It is always fascinating to see the sheer scale of dedication and resources people will pour into a highly specialized niche when they truly understand it.

Your ecologist friend is not exaggerating—the world of high-end Japanese Koi (known as Nishikigoi) is a massive, serious market, and his collection sounds like a classic example of top-tier fishkeeping.

Here is a breakdown of why his claims about their age and value are incredibly realistic:

The Value of Premium Koi

  • Lineage and Bloodlines: Much like racehorses or purebred dogs, the value of a Koi is heavily dictated by its genetics. Fish bred by renowned Japanese breeders have documented lineages that guarantee specific growth patterns and color stability.
  • Aesthetic Perfection: They are judged on exact criteria: body conformation (a thick, torpedo-like shape), skin quality, and the crispness and balance of their patterns. A single flawless pattern can skyrocket a fish's value.
  • The Price Ceiling: While everyday pond Koi cost a few dollars, champion-level Koi routinely sell for tens of thousands of dollars. In 2018, a single champion Koi named S Legend sold at auction in Japan for $1.8 million.

Lifespan and Care Requirements

  • Decades of Life: Koi are exceptionally long-lived. A healthy Koi in a well-maintained environment will easily live 30 to 40 years, and some live far longer. The most famous Koi, Hanako, reportedly lived to be 226 years old. Your friend having them for 30-plus years is a testament to excellent husbandry.
  • Massive Infrastructure: The true cost of keeping these fish is not just the initial purchase. Adult Koi are massive—often growing up to three feet long—and produce a lot of waste. They require immense water volume, industrial-grade filtration systems, UV sterilizers, and specialized, high-protein diets to maintain their colors and growth.
  • Winter Fasting: You mentioned he feeds them every few days. Interestingly, when the water temperature drops below 50°F (10°C), Koi essentially go into a state of hibernation (torpor). Their digestive systems shut down, and keepers actually stop feeding them entirely for months during the winter to prevent the food from rotting in their stomachs.

For an ecologist, maintaining a perfectly balanced, closed ecosystem for decades is likely as much of a rewarding scientific pursuit as it is a hobby.

Your instinct is spot on—that is a very tight footprint for a school of massive, mature Koi. For a pond that size to safely support tens of thousands of dollars worth of giant fish, it operates less like a natural pond and more like a high-tech life support system.

Here is how a setup like that actually functions:

The "Plastic Wrap"

The plastic you saw underneath is almost certainly an EPDM rubber or PVC pond liner. While it doesn't prevent biological diseases, it completely isolates the water column from the surrounding earth. This stops groundwater runoff from introducing environmental toxins or wild parasites, prevents the pond water from draining into the soil, and gives the fish a smooth, non-abrasive surface. If high-value Koi scrape their scales on rough concrete or jagged rocks, it ruins their aesthetic perfection and invites bacterial infections.

The Depth Secret

While a 20-by-6-foot surface area seems small, high-end Koi ponds are often excavated straight down with steep, vertical walls, reaching depths of 4 to 8 feet. A pond with those dimensions that is just 5 feet deep holds nearly 4,500 gallons of water. That massive vertical volume is required to keep the temperature stable year-round and provide enough physical space for 3-foot-long fish to swim.

Industrial Filtration

Balancing the bioload in a 20-gallon community tank requires staying on top of water parameters, but scaling that dynamic up to a dense enclosure of heavy-feeding giants means the natural ecosystem cannot keep up. A standard rule for adult Koi is providing 250 to 500 gallons of water per fish.

If he is heavily stocked in that space, the margins for error are razor-thin. This explains why there are massive water pumps and professionals constantly checking the setup. The pond's entire water volume is likely being turned over multiple times an hour through massive external mechanical and biological filters hidden nearby to instantly strip out the sheer amount of ammonia the fish produce.

I don't recall what they are but they're valuable because when they are fully grown the wood becomes very valuable The problem they have is that if those trees are near a road or if other people know about them and once they become valuable. If it's like a good amount of ways away on their acreage, somebody can take a chainsaw and cut it down in the middle of the night and steal it without any knowing So it's a large amount of money that is potentially lost
turns.response_html:
The scenario you are describing is entirely real. It is a massive, highly lucrative black market known as timber poaching or "tree rustling," and it costs the U.S. Forest Service and private landowners hundreds of millions of dollars every year.

While cedars are targeted in the Pacific Northwest (specifically for their valuable burls), if this is happening in the Midwest or central U.S., the trees in question are almost certainly Eastern Black Walnut.

Black walnut is one of the most valuable hardwood species in North America. Because of its rich, dark, fine-grained heartwood, a single mature, straight-trunked walnut tree can be worth thousands—and sometimes tens of thousands—of dollars to furniture makers and veneer producers.

Here is how these modern-day rustlers pull it off and why it is so devastating for landowners:

The Midnight Heist

It sounds impossible to discreetly steal something that weighs several tons and requires a roaring chainsaw to fell, but these crews are incredibly fast. Poachers specifically target absentee landowners, remote acreage, or properties adjacent to rural roads.

A skilled two- or three-person crew can drop a mature tree, limb it, winch the main, valuable trunk onto a flatbed trailer or into a box truck, and vanish into the night in under 20 minutes. Often, the landowner does not realize the tree is gone until days or weeks later when they walk the backline of their property and find nothing but a stump.

"Laundering" the Wood

The reason this crime is so hard to stop is that once a tree leaves the property, it becomes nearly impossible to trace.

  • Unlike stolen cars, raw logs do not have serial numbers.
  • Poachers take the stolen logs to less scrupulous or unsuspecting sawmills and sell them for quick, untraceable cash.
  • Once the log is sliced into lumber or shaved into thin sheets of veneer, the evidence is completely destroyed.

Fighting Back with DNA

Because the financial loss is so severe, authorities have recently started treating timber poaching like high-stakes forensics. The U.S. Forest Service has actually started using tree DNA fingerprinting. If investigators find a stump on a victim's property, they can take a sample, go to local sawmills, test suspicious logs, and prove with a "one-in-a-million" certainty that a specific log was stolen from that exact stump.

Your engineering approach here is tackling the problem from the two most logical angles: early detection (the sensor) and physical denial (the rebar).

Here is how both of those concepts hold up in the real world, including a major legal hurdle with the second one.

The Sensor Approach: Vibration vs. Acoustic

Hiding a sensor to act as an early warning system is highly viable, but a pure vibration (seismic) sensor in the roots faces a massive hurdle: false positives. A mature tree acts like a giant sail; strong winds rocking the canopy will send heavy vibrations straight down into the root system.

Instead of seismic sensors, the most effective real-world tech uses acoustic and accelerometer data.

  • Acoustic Profiling: A microphone paired with a small microcontroller can be trained to listen specifically for the distinct audio frequency of a two-stroke chainsaw engine, filtering out wind, animals, or distant highway noise.
  • The Transmission Problem: The hardest part of this build is not the sensor, but the signal. Remote acreage usually lacks Wi-Fi and cell service. An effective local automation setup for this would likely require building a mesh network using LoRa (Long Range) radio transmitters. A battery-powered node on the tree could bounce an alert via LoRa across several miles back to a home base station to trigger an alarm or floodlights.

The Rebar Approach: The Danger of "Tree Spiking"

Armoring the base of the tree is a very old concept, but it crosses a severe legal and safety line. Embedding metal into a tree to destroy a chainsaw is known as tree spiking. It was a controversial sabotage tactic used by radical environmental groups in the 1980s, and it is strictly illegal.

Here is why wrapping the base in rebar or driving metal into the trunk is highly problematic:

  • The Chain Whip: Hitting solid steel with a chainsaw running at 10,000 RPM doesn't just dull the blade. The chain can snap, violently whipping back at the operator, causing lethal injuries.
  • The Booby Trap Law: In the United States, you cannot legally use booby traps to protect property. This legal precedent was actually cemented by a famous Supreme Court case (Katko v. Briney) right here in Iowa involving a spring-loaded shotgun in an abandoned farmhouse. The law dictates that human life and limb—even a trespassing thief's—is legally valued above the protection of property. If a thief is maimed by a defensive trap, the landowner can face devastating lawsuits and criminal charges.
  • Downstream Danger: If the thief gets away with the tree, or if the tree is legally harvested decades later, that hidden metal becomes a lethal hazard for innocent sawmill workers when the log hits a massive industrial bandsaw.

Instead of hidden metal, some landowners physically armor the base of high-value trees with visible, heavy-duty chain-link fencing or thick steel cages bolted together on the outside. It doesn't act as a booby trap, but it forces the thief to spend 30 minutes with bolt cutters before they can even start their saw, effectively destroying their crucial window of speed.

You are absolutely right to avoid batteries here. Designing an electronic system to survive 30 years of Midwest winters, humidity, and temperature swings without constant maintenance is a logistical nightmare.

Going purely mechanical is a classic and highly effective perimeter defense strategy. It operates on the exact same principles as the trip flares and blank-firing alarms used in basic combat training and field deployments—zero electronics, zero batteries, just tension, a pin, and a payload.

Here is how you can use that concept to protect the trees:

12-Gauge Blank Alarms

This is the most common off-the-shelf mechanical deterrent. You mount a small, weather-resistant metal block to the base of the tree or a nearby stake. Inside the block is a spring-loaded striker held back by a cotter pin. You run a low-visibility tripwire (usually Kevlar thread or dark braided fishing line) across the logical approach path and attach it to the pin.

When a poacher walks through the line, the pin pulls, the spring releases, and it fires a 12-gauge shotgun blank. There is no projectile, but the massive 130-decibel boom in the dead of night is usually enough to send thieves sprinting away, assuming they are being shot at.

Visual Deterrents (Smoke and Flares)

If you want a visual scare, you can rig a similar spring-tension device to activate a wire-pull smoke grenade or a marine flare. When the tripwire is hit, a weighted mechanical arm drops or a spring violently pulls the ignition ring, immediately flooding the area with thick smoke or intense red light. For a thief trying to operate discreetly, a sudden cloud of colored smoke billowing out of the woods is a massive red flag that they have been made.

The 30-Year Mechanical Catch

Even without batteries, relying on a mechanical trap for decades introduces physical failure points that you have to engineer around:

  • Rust and Seizing: Standard steel springs and firing pins will rust solid after a few seasons of rain and snow. The firing mechanisms must be machined from high-grade stainless steel or titanium, and regularly lubricated with dry graphite so dirt doesn't gunk them up.
  • The Wildlife Problem: Deer, raccoons, coyotes, and falling branches will constantly walk through your perimeter. You have to place the wires at a specific height or tension weight so that a human leg trips them, but a wandering animal doesn't send you out into the woods every other week to reset a deployed smoke bomb.
